title: Effects of a 12-week gait retraining program on the Achilles tendon adaptation of habitually shod runners
publisher: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
claims: Thirty male recreational runners who habitually wore cushioned shoes with a rearfoot strike were recruited and randomised to a retraining group (n=15) or a control group (n=15); 28 completed the study.
The retraining group was asked to run in five-finger minimalist shoes with a forefoot strike three times per week for 12 weeks.
After training, 57% (8/14) of the retraining group shifted from rearfoot to forefoot strike, and the retraining group's foot strike angle was reduced; not all were categorised as forefoot strike.

The abstract reports a significant main effect for time in time-to-peak Achilles tendon force, average Achilles tendon force and peak Achilles tendon loading rate; it does not report a change in peak force itself.
The authors describe the findings as preliminary evidence that a 12-week gait retraining programme could exert a beneficial effect on the Achilles tendon for mechanical loading.
